content: Fractional freezing is a technique employed in process engineering and chemistry to separate two liquids with distinct melting points. This can be achieved through partial melting of a solid, such as in the zone refining of silicon or metals, or by partial crystallization of a liquid, as seen in processes like freeze distillation, also referred to as normal freezing or progressive freezing. Partial crystallization can also be induced by adding a diluent solvent to the mixture, followed by cooling and concentrating the mixture through solvent evaporation, a method known as solution crystallization. Fractional freezing is commonly used to produce ultra-pure solids or to concentrate heat-sensitive liquids. Freeze distillation is a process that enriches a solution by partially freezing it and removing the frozen material, which contains a lower concentration of the dissolved substance compared to the remaining liquid. This enrichment is conceptually similar to traditional distillation, where the evaporated and recondensed portion is richer in the desired component than the liquid left behind. However, this analogy is not entirely accurate, as the thermodynamic principles governing the process are more complex. In the context of freeze distillation, freezing typically begins at a temperature significantly below 0°C. The first material to freeze is not pure water but a dilute solution of alcohol in water. The remaining liquid becomes progressively richer in alcohol, and subsequent freezing occurs at increasingly lower temperatures. The frozen material, while always poorer in alcohol than the liquid, becomes progressively richer in alcohol as the process continues. However, further stages of freezing and removal of frozen material will eventually cease to be effective once the liquid uniformly cools to the temperature of the cooling source. If progressively colder temperatures are available, the frozen material will contain higher concentrations of alcohol, and the fraction of the original alcohol removed with the solid material will increase. In practice, the degree of concentration achieved depends more on the final temperature reached than on the number of cycles of freezing and removal. Thermodynamic principles assure that even at temperatures below the freezing point of ethyl alcohol, a liquid mixture of alcohol and water will persist. At some even lower temperature, the remaining alcohol-water solution will freeze entirely, without yielding a separable alcohol-poor solid. While freeze distillation cannot achieve alcohol concentrations comparable to those obtained through traditional distillation, it is a simpler and less labor-intensive method. However, freeze distillation of alcoholic beverages is illegal in many countries because it concentrates toxic by-products of fermentation, such as fusel alcohols, to potentially harmful levels. Well-known freeze-distilled beverages include applejack and ice beer. Ice wine, on the other hand, is produced through a similar process, but the freezing occurs before fermentation, concentrating sugar rather than alcohol. When purifying solids, two scenarios can arise. If the contaminant is soluble in the desired solid, multiple stages of fractional freezing are required, analogous to multistage distillation. If a eutectic system forms (similar to an azeotrope in distillation), a very pure solid can be obtained, provided the liquid is not at its eutectic composition. If the liquid is at or above its eutectic composition, a mixed solid or an undesired solid may form, complicating separation. Fractional freezing is also used to concentrate liquid phases, particularly in applications where heating is undesirable, such as in the production of fruit juice concentrates and other heat-sensitive liquids. This method avoids the thermal degradation associated with evaporation-based concentration techniques.
